We are a team consisting of high school students with low experience AND expectations, while having a complex relationship with Aerospace, Machine Learning and Data Analysis. Make sure to join us if you want to have a fun learning experience while experimenting with advanced topics! 

But keep in mind... Time does pass differently when you're a "Singularity" :)
summary: PrF-G (Prevent Fire-Guard Neural Network) is the first non-blackbox, MLP-powered neural network that can properly function inside a spaceship without insecure decisions. It functions as an onboard pre-fire margin assistant for crewed spacecraft and lunar habitats. By studying 5 already telemeterized key factors (oxygen concentration, airflow speed, total pressure, information about exposed materials, gravity), it calculates and offers suggestions that can help astronauts fix the damage before it happens. The collected data is compared with a curated database of NASA flight and drop-tower fire experiments, including 70 flight runs, 6 drop-tower limit points, 22 investigations and 30 materials. The project categorizes, ranks and creates a hierarchy among the importance of the data (NOMINAL, REDUCED, UNVERIFIED, LOW and UNTESTED) and presents them to the astronaut in a simple and understandable way. The PrF-G dashboard proposes the most relevant solution to each potentially aggravating variable. For example, if oxygen starts drifting up, it projects when the cabin will leave NASA’s tested range and suggests a fix. The groundbreaking advantage of the idea is that it fixes NASA's current AI problem by only adding the network on top of already existing telemetry instead of replacing the current interpretation of the metrics, making it work as a safe overlay that never acts without permission rather than an independent agent that controls the spaceship, which has many risks.
details:
PrF-G — Project Details

Overview

PrF-G (Prevent Fire-Guard Neural Network) is an onboard pre-fire margin assistant for crewed spacecraft and lunar habitats. It brings a neural network into the cabin without the black-box risk: the network works as an overlay on top of existing telemetry and an evidence-based core, so it can inform the crew but can never take a decision. The question PrF-G answers, continuously and before anything burns, is: has NASA ever tested this cabin, with these materials, at these conditions?

It reads five variables the vehicle already measures: oxygen concentration, total pressure, airflow speed, gravity and the exposed cabin materials. It compares them with NASA fire experiments and shows one status, a one-sentence reason, the NASA tests behind it, and fixes the crew can approve. PrF-G is advisory only: it never changes the atmosphere, never silences an alarm and never fights a fire. We built it for NASA Space Apps 2026, challenge "Flame in Freefall".

The problem

Spacecraft fire protection starts once something is already burning. ISS smoke detectors trigger power, ventilation and oxygen shutdown, but nothing warns the crew that conditions are drifting into territory no material was ever tested in. Detection is also unreliable: dust caused more than 20 automatic fire responses on the ISS in six years, all false, and detectors are switched off during dusty work.

Future missions widen the gap. Exploration cabins will run at higher oxygen and lower pressure, NASA has no fire data at all for lunar or Martian gravity, and on the way to Mars every answer from Mission Control takes many minutes. The data that could help is public but scattered across reports and appendices.

How it works

Evidence base. 76 records (70 flight runs and 6 drop-tower limit points) from BASS-II, Saffire I to V, NASA/TM-2008-215260 and more. Missing values stay "not reported", and we never mix 1 g with microgravity, ignition with sustained burning, or limit tests with spread tests.

Statuses. For each exposed material PrF-G finds supporting evidence, or says "untested" and shows the highest oxygen NASA ever tested it at. The cabin then gets one status:

Status

Alert

Meaning

NOMINAL

none

Every exposed material has NASA evidence here

REDUCED

Advisory

Part of the cabin is untested, or oxygen or airflow is in a sensitive range

UNVERIFIED

Advisory

No exposed material has NASA evidence here

LOW

Caution

Oxygen is outside the reference range, or above its band with most of the cabin untested

Flame spread. A Gaussian process fitted to 39 BASS-II segments predicts PMMA spread within a typical factor of 1.25, and refuses to answer outside its tested range.

Options and trend. PrF-G proposes fixes with their projected effect, such as "Return O₂ to the design point: LOW to UNVERIFIED", and the crew approves or declines each. An 8-minute O₂ trend projects separately when the cabin reaches the caution point and when it leaves NASA's tested range.

Alerts. Following ISS, NASA and aviation guidance, a notice appears only when the status changes, explains itself, can be spoken aloud and stays until acknowledged. Acknowledging never counts as fixing.

The black-box problem, solved by design

AI is kept out of safety-critical systems because a neural network cannot explain its outputs: if it decides, nobody can check why. PrF-G removes that risk by architecture instead of by trust. Every status, alert and crew option comes from traceable rules and NASA test data. The neural network runs beside that core as an overlay: it reads the same telemetry, adds a second opinion, and has no path to any decision.

  • Separated by design. Nothing in the evidence engine reads the network's output, and an automated test confirms on every build that calling the network never changes the status.
  • Visible disagreement. The dashboard shows the NASA evidence and the network's opinion side by side for each material. When they disagree, the crew sees both, and the status still follows the evidence.
  • No number without evidence. Outside its training range (for example oxygen above 26.2%, low pressure or partial gravity) the network withholds its score and says "untested".
  • Safe to load. Weights ship as NumPy arrays and JSON, never as pickle files that can execute code.

The network itself is a multilayer perceptron (16 hidden units, written in NumPy) trained with grouped cross-validation on the NASA runs to judge whether a material would keep burning. Because it is an overlay, it adds information where it is useful and cannot cause harm where it is wrong. The crew stays in control at all times.

The demo

A full-screen mission simulator with four routes: lunar surface (0.166 g), space station, lunar outpost and Mars (0.38 g). Before launch, the crew sets the atmospheres, materials, cabin volume and structural limit, and a pre-flight check shows the status each phase will have.

To show why early warning matters, the demo can follow an ignored caution all the way to loss of the vehicle. Ignition follows an unresolved caution, the fire grows by standard fire-engineering curves, and the outcome is judged only against NASA limits: cabin pressure (NASA-STD-3001), carbon monoxide (JSC 20584) and the 29 psia at which Apollo 204 ruptured. A loss report then shows when PrF-G warned and what would have prevented it.

Benefits and impact

  • Warning before a fire, while fixing it is still easy.
  • Honest about gaps: "untested" instead of a confident guess, every answer linked to its NASA source.
  • Less reliance on Mission Control, which becomes essential on the way to Mars.
  • No new hardware: it uses telemetry spacecraft already collect, and works offline.
  • A research map: the conditions PrF-G keeps marking "untested" are the experiments future missions need most.

What makes it different

  • It measures the evidence, not the fire. Most fire tools try to detect a fire or predict a probability. PrF-G asks "has this been tested?" and treats the edge of NASA's data as a safety margin in its own right, so it cannot overstate what is known.
  • "Untested" is a real answer. Instead of hiding gaps behind an average, PrF-G puts them on screen, in partial gravity, at high oxygen and at low pressure.
  • AI as an overlay, not a decision maker. The neural network can disagree, and the crew sees it disagree, but it cannot change what happens.
  • Consequences are shown, not told. The demo places PrF-G's warning and the failure on the same timeline, with every metric against its NASA limit.
  • One tool, many spacecraft. Atmospheres, materials, cabin volume and structural limits are inputs, so the same PrF-G screens a station, a capsule, an outpost and a Mars habitat.

Tools

TypeScript, React and Vite for the simulator; Python, FastAPI and NumPy for the backend and models; scikit-learn for cross-validation; Playwright for browser tests; GitHub, Render and Cloudflare for deployment. We used Claude (Anthropic) to help write code and documentation; the concept, data verification, rules and neural network are our own, and every number traces to a cited source.

Limits and next steps

The evidence base is small and there is no partial-gravity fire data, so lunar and Martian habitats always show "untested". Telemetry in the demo is simulated, and fire growth in the consequence model uses standard engineering values because NASA has not measured whole-cabin fires. Next: more NASA data as it is published, real telemetry, and testing the alerts with astronauts and flight controllers.
